title: Logical computation with canonical lifted product codes
authors: Han Zheng, Guo Zheng, Liang Jiang, Qian Xu
abstract: High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes encode many logical qubits with low physical-qubit overhead, but realizing efficient fault-tolerant computation on such dense encodings remains a major challenge. Generic, code-agnostic techniques such as code surgery and gate teleportation apply broadly, but are difficult to make modular, low-overhead, and fully certifiable on complex high-rate codes whose structure is left unexploited. Here we overcome these obstacles by co-designing the code together with its logical instruction set for a broad family of \emph{canonical} lifted-product (LP) codes with cyclic symmetry. We show that these codes admit a \emph{canonical logical basis}, in which conjugate logical operators are organized into rows and columns of cyclic orbits inherited directly from the underlying classical codes, analogous to the structure that makes hypergraph-product codes so tractable. This canonical basis unlocks a complete logical instruction set, including constant-depth automorphism and fold-transversal Clifford gates, modular graph code surgeries built from a constant number of reusable seed surgery gadgets or a compact canonical extractor, highly parallel logical Pauli-product measurements, and parallel magic-state injection. For example, a $[[1122,148,\leq\!20]]$ (resp. $[[4350,1224,\leq\!20]]$) LP code requires only two (resp. four) seed surgery gadgets, while arbitrary high-weight logical measurements can be implemented using a full extractor smaller than half of the data code block. These results advance the frontier of fault-tolerant quantum computation on ultra-high-rate quantum architectures.
summary: This paper presents a theoretical framework to enable fault-tolerant quantum computation on advanced high-rate qLDPC codes by co-designing the code with its logic. By establishing a 'canonical logical basis' exploiting inherent symmetries, they derive a complete set of modular and low-overhead gates. This advances the feasibility of building large-scale quantum processors using these highly efficient error-correcting codes.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing efficient, fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols for high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes beyond simple state storage.
main_result: The authors show that canonical lifted-product (LP) codes admit a structured 'canonical logical basis' which unlocks a complete, modular logical instruction set for universal fault-tolerant computation.
method: They co-design the code structure with its logical operations by exploiting inherent symmetries to derive this canonical basis and associated low-overhead gadgets.
model_or_system: The work focuses on high-rate qLDPC codes, specifically a family of canonical lifted-product (LP) codes defined over cyclic group rings. These codes are designed for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
key_observables: Logical qubits ($\overline{q}_{i,j,m}$), code distances ($d$), and the efficiency/overhead of logical operations (e.g., seed gadget size).
important_parameters: High encoding rates, low physical-qubit overhead, and the ability to perform parallel measurements and state injections.
main_assumptions: The framework relies on 'mild algebraic conditions' for the LP codes to be canonical; residual operators are assumed to be gauge logical operators.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the code structure, basis, and resulting instruction set. Table I summarizes the full logical instruction set (action, space/time cost).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the LP code framework, derives the canonical logical basis exploiting symmetries, details the complete logical instruction set (automorphisms, Clifford gates, measurements), and finally provides resource analysis for key components like seed surgery gadgets.
why_interesting: While focused on abstract coding theory, the development of highly structured, low-overhead logical operations is crucial for any physical platform attempting large-scale quantum computation, including those based on trapped ions or superconducting circuits.
